title: Proxy
summary: A proxy is an intermediary that receives a client request, applies policy, and forwards that request to the destination on the client's behalf, so the client never communicates directly with the remote server. Forward proxies serve outbound traffic and are the classic control point for URL filtering, malware blocking, authentication, logging and caching, while reverse proxies sit in front of servers to terminate TLS, balance load and shield applications from direct exposure. Because a forward proxy sees the full request, including hostname, path, headers and, where transport encryption is terminated, the body, it can enforce category and content rules that a packet filter cannot express. Proxies are also a natural place for authentication, so access decisions can be tied to a user identity rather than an address, and for inspecting protocols that negotiate their own transfers, such as web traffic carrying file downloads or application programming interface calls. The operational challenges are bypass and scale. Applications that ignore system proxy settings, mobile devices that roam off the corporate network, and encrypted protocols on non-standard ports can all sidestep a proxy unless it is combined with egress control that blocks direct outbound connections, so enforcement of proxy use matters more than the feature list. Explicit proxies require client configuration, while transparent interception redirects traffic without client knowledge, which simplifies rollout but breaks certificate-pinned applications and creates privacy obligations. High availability is essential because an inline proxy failure becomes an outage, and capacity must account for decryption overhead. Logging is where the proxy earns its keep: full URLs, identities, response codes, byte counts and file metadata are among the richest sources for detecting beaconing, staged downloads and exfiltration over web services, though the volume makes retention and indexing a real design constraint.
objectives: You will be able to distinguish forward and reverse proxy roles and the controls each enables.
You will be able to triage proxy logs for beaconing, staged payload downloads and exfiltration over web services.
You will be able to compare explicit configuration with transparent interception and their operational trade-offs.
You will be able to design egress control that prevents applications from bypassing the proxy.
You will be able to plan for high availability, capacity and cost limits in a proxy deployment.
You will be able to map proxy telemetry to adversary techniques and state what the logs cannot show.

beginner.definition: A proxy is a middleman for network traffic. Your device sends its request to the proxy, the proxy decides whether to allow it, and then makes the request on your behalf. The remote server never speaks to you directly. Forward proxies handle outbound traffic from users, while reverse proxies stand in front of servers to protect them.
beginner.whyItMatters: A firewall sees addresses and ports, but a proxy can see the full web request, including the site name, the page and the file being downloaded. That extra detail lets you block whole categories of sites and spot a machine quietly sending data out. Proxies also tie access to a person's account rather than an address, so the rules follow the user everywhere. The catch is that anything which ignores the proxy bypasses it completely.
howItWorks: You configure devices, or the network, so web requests go to the proxy first.
The proxy checks who the user is and what category the site belongs to.
If policy allows it, the proxy fetches the page and returns it to the user.
It logs the address, the user, the site, the file details and how much data moved.
For encrypted sites, the proxy may need to decrypt before it can read anything.
You then block direct outbound connections, so nothing can skip the proxy.
beginner.example: Think of a company mail room. Every letter leaves through it, and the staff there check the address, note it in a log and refuse anything on the banned list. Senders never hand letters directly to the post office. If someone climbs out of a window and posts a letter themselves, the mail room never sees it. That is why forcing all traffic through the proxy matters as much as the proxy itself.
takeaways: A proxy sits in the middle and can read the whole web request.
It ties rules to user accounts, not just to network addresses.
If traffic can skip the proxy, the proxy gives you false comfort.

exercises.title: Proxy - EASY
exercises.summary: Recall and recognition: definitions, one clear answer, single-step questions.

exercises.title: Proxy - MEDIUM
exercises.summary: Application: read a short log or alert and choose the correct next step.

exercises.title: Proxy - HARD
exercises.summary: Analysis: a multi-step scenario with distractors, evidence to weigh, and a reason to give.

exercises.title: Proxy - EXTREMELY HARD
exercises.summary: Synthesis under pressure: incomplete evidence, competing priorities, and a decision you must defend.
